primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Pycnodysostosis due to CTSK loss of function
mechanism: Cathepsin K is a lysosomal cysteine protease highly expressed in osteoclasts that degrades type I and II collagen and other bone-matrix proteins in the acidic resorption compartment. CTSK loss impairs organic bone-matrix degradation, increasing bone density while making bone brittle.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy has short stature and several fractures after minor trauma. Radiographs show generalized osteosclerosis, acro-osteolysis of the distal phalanges, and persistent open cranial sutures. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in CTSK. Osteoclast number is normal.
lead: Which of the following cellular abnormalities most directly explains this child's increased bone density?
correct: Impaired osteoclast degradation of collagenous bone matrix within acidic resorption compartments
distractors: Failure of osteoclast proton secretion due to loss of the vacuolar H+-ATPase
Failure of RANK signaling resulting in absent osteoclast differentiation
Reduced tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase activity causing extracellular pyrophosphate accumulation
Defective type I collagen triple-helix formation by osteoblasts
distractor_notes: Vacuolar proton-pump defects can cause osteopetrosis by preventing acidification and mineral dissolution. In pycnodysostosis, osteoclasts are present and the distinctive defect is cathepsin-K-mediated organic matrix degradation.
Defective RANK/RANKL signaling can cause osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis. The stem explicitly states that osteoclast number is normal.
ALPL deficiency causes hypophosphatasia with impaired mineralization and low bone mineralization, not osteosclerosis from failure to degrade collagen matrix.
Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta with fragile low-density bone rather than CTSK-related osteosclerosis and acro-osteolysis.
key_expl: Pycnodysostosis is caused by loss-of-function variants in CTSK. Cathepsin K is an osteoclast lysosomal cysteine protease that degrades collagen and other proteins of the organic bone matrix at low pH. Osteoclast numbers and ruffled borders can be preserved, but matrix degradation is impaired, leading to increased bone density with brittle bones and characteristic skeletal findings.
objective: Explain pycnodysostosis as impaired cathepsin-K-mediated degradation of collagenous bone matrix by otherwise present osteoclasts.
